notes.front: What is a host-based intrusion detection system (HIDS)?
notes.back: A system that monitors the characteristics of a single host, and the events occurring within it, for suspicious activity.
notes.explanation: Its scope is set by the words “host-based”: one host and what happens inside it, not a whole network segment.
notes.example: Like a smoke detector fitted in one flat, rather than one watching the whole building’s ventilation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems, §7 “Host-Based IDPS”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: A host-based IDPS monitors the characteristics of a single host and the events occurring within that host for suspicious activity.

notes.front: What is a host-based intrusion prevention system (HIPS)?
notes.back: Host-based agent software that monitors one host and, when prevention capabilities are enabled, also takes prevention actions on it.
notes.explanation: The same kind of host agent does both jobs: detection always, and prevention actions once those capabilities are switched on.
notes.example: Like a door steward who not only notes a suspicious visitor but can also refuse them entry.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems, PDF p. 82
notes.evidence: Each agent monitors activity on a single host and if prevention capabilities are enabled, also performs prevention actions.

notes.front: What is a host-based firewall?
notes.back: A software firewall residing on the host it protects, monitoring and controlling that single host’s incoming and outgoing network traffic.
notes.explanation: The guidance presents host-based and personal firewalls as an additional layer of security against network-based attacks.
notes.example: Like a lock on your own office door as well as the lock on the building’s front entrance.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2.2.1 “Host-Based Firewalls and Personal Firewalls”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Host-based firewalls for servers and personal firewalls for desktop and laptop personal computers (PC) provide an additional layer of security against network-based attacks. These firewalls are software-based, residing on the hosts they are protecting—each monitors and controls the incoming and outgoing network traffic for a single host.

notes.front: What is application whitelisting?
notes.back: Using a list of authorised applications and components to control which applications are permitted to install or execute on a host.
notes.explanation: The whitelist covers application components such as libraries and configuration files, not only programs, and is measured against a well-defined baseline.
notes.example: Like a staff canteen till that accepts only the payment cards on its approved list.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: An application whitelist is a list of applications and application components (libraries, configuration files, etc.) that are authorized to be present or active on a host according to a well-defined baseline. The technologies used to apply application whitelists—to control which applications are permitted to install or execute on a host—are called whitelisting programs

notes.front: What is full disk encryption (FDE)?
notes.back: Encrypting all the data on the drive used to boot a computer, including its operating system, with access only after authenticating to the FDE product.
notes.explanation: It is also known as whole disk encryption; the operating system itself is part of what is encrypted.
notes.example: Like a safe whose entire contents stay locked until the right combination is entered at the door.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.1.1 “Full Disk Encryption”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Full disk encryption (FDE), also known as whole disk encryption, is the process of encrypting all the data on the hard drive used to boot a computer, including the computer’s OS, and permitting access to the data only after successful authentication to the FDE product.

notes.front: What is endpoint detection and response (EDR)?
notes.back: Solutions that collect security telemetry data on endpoints, giving security teams visibility into activity there.
notes.explanation: The guidance notes that most traffic is now east-west, within the local network, and largely invisible to security teams; EDR is one way visibility is sought.
notes.example: Like a flight recorder on every aircraft, rather than relying only on radar at the airport.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: However, over 75 % of network traffic is now east-west (i.e., within the local network) or server-to-server (due to applications being based on microservices), which is largely invisible to security teams, though some visibility is now sought through endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions that collect security telemetry data on endpoints.

notes.front: What is corporate-owned, personally enabled (COPE)?
notes.back: A mobile deployment model in which the enterprise issues and owns (or leases) the device but allows employees some personal use of it.
notes.explanation: The enterprise still enforces usage restrictions, but they are more lenient than in a work-only model.
notes.example: Like a company car that you may also use for the weekend shopping.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.2 “Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled (COPE)”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: COPE devices are issued by the enterprise to employees. The COPE model is less restrictive on employee personal use. While the enterprise owns (or leases) the device and enforces usage restrictions, these restrictions are more lenient, allowing employees some personal use of the device.

notes.front: What is bring your own device (BYOD)?
notes.back: A deployment model that lets employees use their personally owned mobile devices to access enterprise data and services.
notes.explanation: Personal and enterprise use then mix on one device: an employee may reach personal and sensitive enterprise email through the same app.
notes.example: Like a courier who does deliveries on their own bicycle instead of a company van.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.3 “BYOD and Choose Your Own Device (CYOD)”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: The BYOD deployment model allows employees to use their personally owned mobile devices to access enterprise data and services. The employee may, for example, access both personal email and sensitive enterprise email via the same application.

notes.front: What is mobile device management (MDM)?
notes.back: Enterprise management of the whole mobile device, which requires the owner to enrol it under enterprise management and accept an enterprise profile on it.
notes.explanation: Enrolment and an installed enterprise profile are the two things the guidance says device management asks of the owner and application-level management does not.
notes.example: Like a landlord who keeps a master key to every room of the flat.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.2 “Mobile Application Management”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: Unlike MDMs, MAM systems do not require the device owner to enroll the device under enterprise management, nor must the owner accept installation of an enterprise profile on the device.

notes.front: What is enterprise mobility management (EMM)?
notes.back: A solution used to deploy, configure and actively manage mobile devices in an enterprise; a suite may include MDM, application management and threat defence.
notes.explanation: It is the umbrella product: the guidance says a suite may encompass device management, application management, mobile threat defence and other technologies.
notes.example: Like a facilities contract that covers locks, cleaning and repairs under one provider.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.1 “Enterprise Mobility Management”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: EMM, which is sometimes referred to as UEM (unified endpoint management), is a solution used to deploy, configure, and actively manage mobile devices in an enterprise environment. An EMM suite may encompass mobile device management (MDM), mobile application management (MAM), MTD, and other management technologies.

notes.front: What is mobile application management (MAM)?
notes.back: Enterprise control over the mobile apps that access enterprise services or data, without requiring the owner to enrol the device.
notes.explanation: It governs apps, both privately developed and publicly available, rather than the whole device as MDM does.
notes.example: Like a landlord who holds the key to the shared office room only, leaving the tenant’s own rooms alone.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.2 “Mobile Application Management”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: MAM systems are designed to enable enterprise control over mobile apps that access enterprise services and/or data. These apps include privately developed apps and publicly available apps. Unlike MDMs, MAM systems do not require the device owner to enroll the device under enterprise management

notes.front: What are two characteristics of a host that a HIDS might monitor?
notes.back: Any two of: that host’s network traffic, system logs, running processes, file access and modification, system and application configuration changes.
notes.explanation: These are examples, not a closed list, and network traffic counts only as it concerns that one host.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems, §7 “Host-Based IDPS”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: Examples of the types of characteristics a host-based IDPS might monitor are wired and wireless network traffic (only for that host), system logs, running processes, file access and modification, and system and application configuration changes.

notes.front: Which host-based prevention technique can stop code, including malware and unauthorised applications, from being executed?
notes.back: Code analysis.
notes.explanation: If configured and tuned well, it can be very effective, particularly at stopping previously unknown attacks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems, §7.2.3 “Prevention Capabilities”, PDF p. 80
notes.evidence: The code analysis techniques can prevent code from being executed, including malware and unauthorized applications. Some host-based IDPSs can also stop network applications from invoking shells, which could be used to attempt to perform certain types of attacks. If configured and tuned well, code analysis can be very effective, particularly at stopping previously unknown attacks.

notes.front: A server’s host-based firewall allows only necessary traffic. Against traffic from which hosts does that protect it?
notes.back: All hosts, including those on the same subnet or on other internal subnets not separated by a network firewall.
notes.explanation: The filtering happens at the server itself, so it applies whichever subnet the traffic comes from.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2.2.1 “Host-Based Firewalls and Personal Firewalls”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Configuring a hostbased firewall to allow only necessary traffic to the server provides protection against malicious activity from all hosts, including those on the same subnet or on other internal subnets not separated by a network firewall.

notes.front: How does application whitelisting differ in approach from antivirus software?
notes.back: Antivirus blocks known bad activity and permits everything else; whitelisting permits known good activity and blocks everything else.
notes.explanation: Whitelisting is intended to stop malware and other unauthorised software from executing, without first having to recognise it as bad.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Application whitelisting technologies are intended to stop the execution of malware and other unauthorized software. Unlike security technologies such as antivirus software, which block known bad activity and permit all other, application whitelisting technologies are designed to permit known good activity and block all other.

notes.front: In application whitelisting, what does audit mode do?
notes.back: Lets items run, including those not on the whitelist, and logs their execution.
notes.explanation: The logs give continuous monitoring processes data to analyse.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.3 “Application Whitelisting Modes”, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: Audit mode allows items, including those not on the whitelist to be executed and logs their execution. This mode provides data for continuous monitoring processes to analyze.

notes.front: In application whitelisting, what does enforcement mode do?
notes.back: Automatically permits execution of whitelisted items and/or blocks execution of blacklisted items.
notes.explanation: Unlike audit mode, it acts on the lists instead of only recording what runs.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.3 “Application Whitelisting Modes”, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: Enforcement mode automatically permits execution of whitelisted items and/or blocks execution of blacklisted items.

notes.front: Which whitelisting attribute permits every application in a given directory, and is very weak used by itself?
notes.back: File path.
notes.explanation: It lets any malicious file placed in the directory run; strict access controls that let only authorised administrators add or modify files make it stronger.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.2.1 “File and Folder Attributes”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: to permit all applications contained within a particular path (directory/folder). Used by itself, this is a very weak attribute, because it allows any malicious files placed within the directory to be executed. However, if the path is protected by strict access controls that only allow authorized administrators to add or modify files, this becomes a stronger attribute.

notes.front: Which whitelisting attribute still lets a file run after it has been infected or replaced, because that detail does not change?
notes.back: Filename.
notes.explanation: An attacker could also simply place a malicious file on the host under the name of a common benign file.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.2.1 “File and Folder Attributes”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: If a file were to become infected or be replaced, its name would be unchanged so the file would still be executed under the whitelist. Also, an attacker could simply place a malicious file onto a host and use the same name as a common benign file.

notes.front: Which whitelisting attribute assumes a malicious version of an application would differ in length from the original?
notes.back: File size.
notes.explanation: It is typically used only in combination with other attributes, and attackers can craft malicious files of the same length as benign ones.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.2.1 “File and Folder Attributes”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: This attribute is typically used only in combination with other attributes, such as filename. Monitoring the file size assumes that a malicious version of an application would have a different file size than the original; however, attackers can craft malicious files to have the same length as their benign counterparts.

notes.front: Which whitelisting attribute, if based on the vendor’s verified identity alone, would let older software versions with known vulnerabilities run?
notes.back: Digital signature or publisher.
notes.explanation: Its benefit is low upkeep: the whitelist needs updating only for a new publisher or when a publisher updates its signature key.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.2.1 “File and Folder Attributes”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Also, relying on the publisher’s verified identity only would allow older software versions with known vulnerabilities to be executed. However, the benefit of basing a whitelist on publisher identities is that the whitelist only needs updates when there is a new publisher (i.e., software vendor) or when a publisher updates its signature key.

notes.front: Which whitelisting attribute stays accurate however a file is placed, named or signed, but is unhelpful once the file is patched?
notes.back: Cryptographic hash.
notes.explanation: Updates such as patches are its weak point, not renaming, moving or re-signing the file.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.2.1 “File and Folder Attributes”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Cryptographic hashes are accurate no matter where the file is placed, what it is named, or how it is signed. However, a cryptographic hash is not helpful when a file is updated, such as when an application is patched

notes.front: Which combination of whitelisting attributes generally gives the most accurate and comprehensive capability?
notes.back: Digital signature/publisher combined with cryptographic hash.
notes.explanation: The price is effort: usability and maintainability requirements can put significant burdens on the organisation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: A combination of digital signature/publisher and cryptographic hash techniques generally provides the most accurate and comprehensive application whitelisting capability, but usability and maintainability requirements can put significant burdens on the organization.

notes.front: In full disk encryption, what is pre-boot authentication?
notes.back: Authenticating successfully, for example with a username and password, before the operating system is decrypted and booted.
notes.explanation: The prompt comes from the product’s pre-boot environment, before any decryption of the operating system takes place.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.1.1 “Full Disk Encryption”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: The PBE prompts the user to authenticate successfully, such as entering a user ID and password, before decrypting and booting the OS. This is known as pre-boot authentication (PBA).

notes.front: Once a computer protected by full disk encryption has booted, how much protection does FDE give?
notes.back: None: once the operating system is loaded, it becomes fully responsible for protecting the unencrypted information.
notes.explanation: FDE protects all the data on a computer that is not booted, assuming pre-boot authentication is required.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.2 “Protection Provided by Storage Encryption Technologies”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: For a computer that is not booted, all the information encrypted by FDE is protected, assuming that pre-boot authentication is required. When the device is booted, then FDE provides no protection; once the OS is loaded, the OS becomes fully responsible for protecting the unencrypted information.

notes.front: What is virtual disk encryption?
notes.back: Encrypting a container file that can hold many files and folders, opened only after proper authentication, typically by mounting it as a virtual disk.
notes.explanation: Until authentication the container’s contents stay encrypted; the guidance groups it with volume encryption as one class of storage encryption.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.1.2 “Virtual Disk Encryption and Volume Encryption”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Virtual disk encryption is the process of encrypting a file called a container, which can hold many files and folders, and permitting access to the data within the container only after proper authentication is provided, at which point the container is typically mounted as a virtual disk.

notes.front: What is file/folder encryption?
notes.back: Encrypting individual files, or individual folders, on a storage medium, with access to the encrypted data only after proper authentication.
notes.explanation: Some operating systems offer file or folder encryption built in.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.1.3 “File/Folder Encryption”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: File encryption is the process of encrypting individual files on a storage medium and permitting access to the encrypted data only after proper authentication is provided. Folder encryption is very similar to file encryption, only it addresses individual folders instead of files. Some OSs offer built-in file and/or folder encryption capabilities,

notes.front: What are two places where full disk or file/folder encryption products may keep their local keys?
notes.back: Any two of: the local hard drive, a removable flash drive, a cryptographic token, a trusted platform module chip.
notes.explanation: Some products can instead store keys on a central server and retrieve them automatically once the user authenticates.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §4.2 “Design the Solution”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: For some encryption technologies, such as FDE and many file/folder encryption products, there are often several options for key location, including the local hard drive, a USB flash drive, a cryptographic token, or a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) chip.

notes.front: What must a Transport Layer Security client do if the server certificate fails path validation or the name check?
notes.back: Terminate the connection.
notes.explanation: The name check compares the server name or address the client requested with those contained in the server certificate.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, §4.5.1 “Path Validation”, PDF p. 51
notes.evidence: The client shall terminate the TLS connection if path validation fails. Federal agencies shall only use clients that check that the DNS name or IP address (whichever is presented in the client TLS request) matches a DNS name or IP address contained in the server certificate. The client shall terminate the TLS connection if the name check fails.

notes.front: What are two kinds of attack that mobile threat defence, also called mobile EDR, can detect?
notes.back: Any two of: network-based attacks, app-based attacks, platform-based attacks such as rootkits, phishing attacks.
notes.explanation: The list ends “and others”, so it is not complete.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.3.9 “Mobile Threat Defense”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: MTD systems can detect network-based attacks (e.g., MitM that could intercept and redirect or eavesdrop on communications), app-based attacks (e.g., information leakage or malicious, sideloaded apps), platform-based attacks (e.g., rootkits that undermine basic OS functions), phishing attacks (e.g., to steal credentials), and others.

notes.front: On a COPE device, who owns the device and the information on it?
notes.back: The enterprise, even though the device is personally enabled.
notes.explanation: Employees should be told about enterprise restrictions and expect configurations that affect functionality and privacy.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.2 “Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled (COPE)”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: Although a COPE device is personally enabled, the device and the information on the device belong to the enterprise. Employees should be informed about enterprise restrictions and have appropriate expectations of software and device configurations that affect functionality and privacy.

notes.front: What leakage concern does the BYOD model raise?
notes.back: Sensitive enterprise information leaking via the device to untrustworthy third-party back-end systems that communicate with apps on it.
notes.explanation: The concern is where enterprise data goes once it reaches apps on a device the enterprise does not own.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.3 “BYOD and Choose Your Own Device (CYOD)”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: The BYOD model raises concerns regarding leakage of sensitive enterprise information via the device to untrustworthy third-party backend systems that communicate with various apps on the device.

notes.front: How does strict enterprise usage differ from COPE in personal use of an organisation-issued device?
notes.back: Strict enterprise devices are for enterprise use only and strictly limit personal use; COPE allows some personal use.
notes.explanation: Under strict enterprise usage, employees typically carry a separate personal device as well.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.1 “Strict Enterprise Usage”, PDF p. 45
notes.evidence: This section covers enterprise-enabled mobile devices that are provided to employees for enterprise use only. GFE devices strictly limit personal use; employees typically own and carry a separate personal device.

notes.front: What does remote wipe let administrators delete, and from which mobile devices?
notes.back: Enterprise data and applications, on enterprise-owned or employee-owned (BYOD) devices.
notes.explanation: The capability is widely available on smartphones and tablets that run Android or iOS.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.3.3 “Remote/Secure Wipe”, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: Remote wipe enables enterprise system administrators to delete enterprise data and applications on enterprise-owned or employee-owned (BYOD) mobile devices. The remote wipe capability is widely available on mobile devices, such as smartphones and tablets, that support Android or iOS.

notes.front: Why might an enterprise with a BYOD policy use MAM instead of MDM?
notes.back: It may help address users’ privacy concerns about their personal devices.
notes.explanation: Keep the hedge: the guidance says MAM “may help”, not that it removes every privacy concern.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.2 “Mobile Application Management”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: For enterprises with bring your own device (BYOD) policies, the use of MAM functionality instead of MDM may help address users’ privacy concerns regarding their personal devices.

notes.front: What do secure containers on mobile devices provide?
notes.back: Software-based data isolation that segments enterprise applications and information from personal apps and data.
notes.explanation: A common interface is a portal app that opens a suite of business apps such as email, contacts and calendar.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.7 “Secure Containers”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: Secure containers provide software-based data isolation designed to segment enterprise applications and information from personal apps and data. Containers may present multiple user interfaces, one of the most common being a mobile application that acts as a portal to a suite of business productivity apps, such as email, contacts, and calendar.

notes.front: When should whole-device encryption be activated on a mobile device, and what should happen before it is disposed of?
notes.back: Before the device is deployed; before disposal, a factory reset should cryptographically erase all user data.
notes.explanation: Cryptographic erase works by sanitising the drive’s encryption key, which leaves the encrypted user data unreadable.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, PDF p. 57
notes.evidence: Cryptographic erase is accomplished by sanitizing the encryption key for the drive, rendering the encrypted user data unreadable. It is essential to activate whole-device encryption before a device is deployed and to perform a factory reset operation to cryptographically erase all user data before disposing of a device.

notes.front: A team wants to know whenever someone changes configuration files or starts unexpected processes on its public web server, but it does not want anything blocked. Which fits best?
notes.back: A HIDS agent on the server
notes.choices:
A) Full disk encryption on the server
B) A HIDS agent on the server
C) Application whitelisting in enforcement mode
D) A stricter rule set on the internet-edge network firewall
notes.choicesExplained: A protects stored data and does not watch activity. C blocks programs, which the team does not want. D filters traffic at the edge and cannot see processes or file changes on the host.
notes.explanation: Running processes and configuration changes are among the host characteristics a HIDS monitors for suspicious activity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems, §7 “Host-Based IDPS”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: Examples of the types of characteristics a host-based IDPS might monitor are wired and wireless network traffic (only for that host), system logs, running processes, file access and modification, and system and application configuration changes.

notes.front: A finance server’s host agent already alerts on attempts to run unknown programs. The owners now want those attempts stopped automatically. What is the simplest change?
notes.back: Enable the agent’s prevention capabilities so it acts as a HIPS
notes.choices:
A) Send more of the server’s logs to the event management system
B) Replace the agent with a network-only sensor
C) Enable the agent’s prevention capabilities so it acts as a HIPS
D) Move the server to a separate network segment
notes.choicesExplained: A adds visibility but still only alerts. B loses the view of activity on the host. D changes who can reach the server but does not stop a program running on it.
notes.explanation: A host-based agent that has prevention capabilities enabled performs prevention actions as well as monitoring.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems, PDF p. 82
notes.evidence: Each agent monitors activity on a single host and if prevention capabilities are enabled, also performs prevention actions.

notes.front: An infected laptop on the same internal subnet as a database server begins probing it. No network firewall sits between them. Which control on the server itself is meant to block this?
notes.back: A host-based firewall that allows only necessary traffic
notes.choices:
A) A host-based firewall that allows only necessary traffic
B) Application whitelisting
C) The internet-edge network firewall
D) Full disk encryption
notes.choicesExplained: B controls which programs may run, not network traffic. C never sees traffic that stays inside the subnet. D protects stored data, not network connections.
notes.explanation: A host-based firewall allowing only necessary traffic protects the server from all hosts, including those on its own subnet.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2.2.1 “Host-Based Firewalls and Personal Firewalls”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Configuring a hostbased firewall to allow only necessary traffic to the server provides protection against malicious activity from all hosts, including those on the same subnet or on other internal subnets not separated by a network firewall.

notes.front: An attacker copies a malicious program onto a workstation, gives it the name of an approved tool and pads it to the same size. Which single whitelisting attribute would still stop it?
notes.back: Cryptographic hash
notes.choices:
A) Filename
B) File size
C) File path, on a folder all users can write to
D) Cryptographic hash
notes.choicesExplained: A and B match the fake by design. C lets anything in that folder run, and anyone can write there.
notes.explanation: A hash stays accurate whatever the file is called or where it sits, so a look-alike file with different contents does not match.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, §2.2.1 “File and Folder Attributes”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Cryptographic hashes are accurate no matter where the file is placed, what it is named, or how it is signed.

notes.front: A council wants its library kiosks to run only the browser and catalogue app it installed, and nothing a visitor downloads, known threat or not. Which control fits?
notes.back: Application whitelisting
notes.choices:
A) Application whitelisting
B) Antivirus with daily signature updates
C) A host-based firewall
D) Volume encryption
notes.choicesExplained: B blocks only known bad software and lets the rest run. C filters network traffic, not which programs execute. D protects stored data.
notes.explanation: Whitelisting permits known good software and blocks everything else, so an unknown download does not run.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-167, Guide to Application Whitelisting, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Unlike security technologies such as antivirus software, which block known bad activity and permit all other, application whitelisting technologies are designed to permit known good activity and block all other.

notes.front: A field engineer needs one encrypted place on her laptop for several client files. Even their names must stay hidden until she unlocks it. Which technique fits?
notes.back: Virtual disk encryption
notes.choices:
A) File/folder encryption
B) Virtual disk encryption
C) A host-based firewall
D) Application whitelisting
notes.choicesExplained: A is transparent: file names and possibly other metadata stay visible. C and D do not encrypt stored data.
notes.explanation: A virtual disk container is one opaque file: nobody can see what is inside until it is decrypted.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.1.3 “File/Folder Encryption”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: A container is a single opaque file, meaning that no one can see what files or folders are inside the container until the container is decrypted.

notes.front: Two identical laptops use full disk encryption with pre-boot authentication. One is stolen switched off; the other is stolen switched on and unlocked. Which statement is right?
notes.back: The switched-off laptop is protected by FDE; the running one depends on its operating system
notes.choices:
A) Both are fully protected by FDE
B) Neither is protected, because FDE only covers removable media
C) The switched-off laptop is protected by FDE; the running one depends on its operating system
D) Only the hibernation file of each is protected
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that FDE gives no protection once the device has booted. B is wrong: FDE covers the boot drive. D confuses a detail about hibernation with the main protection.
notes.explanation: FDE protects a computer that is not booted, if pre-boot authentication is required; after boot the operating system is responsible.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-111, Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices, §3.2 “Protection Provided by Storage Encryption Technologies”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: For a computer that is not booted, all the information encrypted by FDE is protected, assuming that pre-boot authentication is required. When the device is booted, then FDE provides no protection; once the OS is loaded, the OS becomes fully responsible for protecting the unencrypted information.

notes.front: A browser connects to a payments site and receives a certificate that chains to a trusted root but names a different site. What should the client do?
notes.back: Terminate the connection
notes.choices:
A) Continue, because the chain is valid
B) Continue, but only after checking revocation
C) Accept it for this session only
D) Terminate the connection
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the failed name check. B covers only one of the required checks; the name check has still failed.
notes.explanation: A client must terminate the connection if the name it requested does not match a name in the server certificate.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, §4.5.1 “Path Validation”, PDF p. 51
notes.evidence: The client shall terminate the TLS connection if the name check fails.

notes.front: A company’s perimeter sensors watch traffic entering and leaving its network, but an intruder moving from one internal server to another goes unnoticed. What would give visibility on the servers themselves?
notes.back: EDR collecting security telemetry on each endpoint
notes.choices:
A) A faster internet connection
B) Longer passwords on the edge router
C) EDR collecting security telemetry on each endpoint
D) A cold site
notes.choicesExplained: A and B do nothing for visibility inside the network. D is a recovery facility, not a monitoring tool.
notes.explanation: Traffic between internal servers is largely invisible to perimeter tools; EDR collects telemetry on the endpoints themselves.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: which is largely invisible to security teams, though some visibility is now sought through endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions that collect security telemetry data on endpoints.

notes.front: A firm buys phones for its sales staff, keeps ownership, and lets them install some approved personal apps and receive personal texts. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: COPE
notes.choices:
A) BYOD
B) COPE
C) Strict enterprise usage
D) Virtual desktop infrastructure
notes.choicesExplained: A needs the phones to be the employees’ own. C would strictly limit personal use. D is a way of delivering desktops, not a device ownership model.
notes.explanation: Enterprise ownership with some personal use allowed, such as certain apps or personal texts, is COPE.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.2 “Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled (COPE)”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: For example, an employee may be permitted to download certain apps or receive personal text messages on the COPE device.

notes.front: A consultant reads her client’s enterprise email on a tablet she bought for herself. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: BYOD
notes.choices:
A) COPE
B) Strict enterprise usage
C) BYOD
D) Thin client
notes.choicesExplained: A and B need the organisation to own the device. D describes a kind of terminal, not who owns a mobile device.
notes.explanation: A personally owned device used to access enterprise data and services is BYOD.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §5.1.3.3 “BYOD and Choose Your Own Device (CYOD)”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: The BYOD deployment model allows employees to use their personally owned mobile devices to access enterprise data and services.

notes.front: A charity lets volunteers use their own phones for its rota app. The volunteers refuse to enrol their phones or install an enterprise profile. How can the charity still control the app?
notes.back: MAM
notes.choices:
A) MAM
B) MDM
C) Full disk encryption
D) Strict enterprise usage
notes.choicesExplained: B needs enrolment and an enterprise profile, which the volunteers refuse. C protects stored data but does not control the app. D requires organisation-owned devices.
notes.explanation: MAM controls the apps that reach enterprise services without requiring enrolment or an enterprise profile.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.2 “Mobile Application Management”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: Unlike MDMs, MAM systems do not require the device owner to enroll the device under enterprise management, nor must the owner accept installation of an enterprise profile on the device.

notes.front: A hospital issues tablets and must be able to lock them remotely and wipe them after repeated wrong passcodes. Which approach provides this device-wide control?
notes.back: MDM through the hospital’s EMM
notes.choices:
A) MAM alone
B) Application whitelisting
C) A host-based firewall
D) MDM through the hospital’s EMM
notes.choicesExplained: A manages apps, not the whole device. B controls which programs run. C filters network traffic.
notes.explanation: Remote lock and wiping after failed authentication are device-level policies enforced through EMM technology.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.1.2 “User and Device Authentication”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Under the direction of an administrator, remotely lock the device if it is suspected that the device is lost or was left in an unlocked state in an unsecured location.

notes.front: Staff read work email on personal phones. The company wants work data kept apart from staff photos and personal apps. What design supports this?
notes.back: A secure container separating enterprise apps and data from personal ones
notes.choices:
A) A secure container separating enterprise apps and data from personal ones
B) A host-based firewall on each phone
C) Stricter password ageing
D) Application whitelisting of personal apps
notes.choicesExplained: B filters traffic but does not separate data. C strengthens login only. D limits which apps run but does not isolate enterprise data.
notes.explanation: Secure containers exist to segment enterprise applications and information from personal apps and data.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, §4.2.7 “Secure Containers”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: Secure containers provide software-based data isolation designed to segment enterprise applications and information from personal apps and data.

notes.front: An organisation is retiring 200 encrypted company phones whose keys were never escrowed. What should it do before disposal?
notes.back: Perform a factory reset to cryptographically erase all user data
notes.choices:
A) Delete only the enterprise apps
B) Remove only the phones’ removable cards
C) Update each phone to the newest operating system
D) Perform a factory reset to cryptographically erase all user data
notes.choicesExplained: A and B leave user data on the internal storage. C changes software but erases nothing.
notes.explanation: The guidance calls a factory reset that cryptographically erases all user data essential before disposal.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, PDF p. 57
notes.evidence: It is essential to activate whole-device encryption before a device is deployed and to perform a factory reset operation to cryptographically erase all user data before disposing of a device.
